🇨🇳🛢️ Some [longer] thoughts on Chinese crude oil stock data:

One of the more oil-bearish explanations for China's crude import implosion is that the country simply stopped building stocks, which the official data imply were rising at ~1.5 MMbpd over the prior year, so they needn't rebound to anywhere near where they stood in February. This alone would explain ~2 MMbpd of the 5 MMbpd China import swing.

It's true that China's stocks were rising aggressively, but that official data estimate is *way* too much. It's driven off of official data (National Bureau of Statistics + Customs) on Chinese crude production plus net imports less refining runs. That makes enough sense, but the historical difference is implausibly large. This is likely driven by one of the components being structurally distorted, with my money on official runs being underreported (but there's wiggle with all the major components).

As you can see on the chart on the left, this official data implied build is almost always positive. Even more, if you look at the chart on the right you can see the cumulative implied build since 2017 is nearly **3 billion barrels**

China has built a LOT of crude stocks over the past decade, but the observed crude build based on satellite-derived data (Kpler below) is more like 450 MMbbl at the peak, less than 1/6 of the build implied by official data.

Over the year before the Iran War, observed crude stocks rose by ~375 kbpd vs ~1.4 MMbpd implied by official data, and these observed builds were pretty flat immediately before the Iran War, further blunting the explanatory value for the import swing.

In sum, some of China's crude import pullback can be explained by a halt to prior stockbuilding, but it's likely  a only a modest factor rather than the dominant one.

This is part of ongoing research into China's massive crude import swing, the largest single factor that has thus far blunted the Strait of Hormuz supply shock.

This is understandable given 2027 oversupply concerns but imho a strategic mistake for OPEC+.

The final ~2 MMbpd tranche cut (initiated back in October 2022) is the only full-membership cut and because of that the actual supply that came off was only <1 MMbpd (this was the “paper cut”) due to outdated production baselines. Most members “cut” quota-barrels they couldn’t produce anyway.

As such, this final cut tranche is more bureaucratic headache than it is critical market support.

OPEC+ needs to finally resettle those production baselines because they neuter the production management process, but resetting baselines is a super tricky political process in the best of times—and this is an especially tricky moment given oil market chaos, UAE’s departure from OPEC, Iraq’s threats to follow suit if they don’t get more quota room, etc.

Baseline resetting using consultant estimates is dicey and prone to debate, so OPEC+ should just remove all quotas and let members *prove* what they can produce over, say, 6 months. That’d also necessarily depress crude prices and remind much of the membership of OPEC’s core value.
